narrative:
The model predicted a 50% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability met the school's threshold for risk, your law school application was denied.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your third-year grades had the strongest influence, pushing the prediction toward failure. While your first-year performance placed you at the average decile for accepted students, your third-year decile dropped noticeably below the accepted-student average. This decline signaled to the model a weakening academic trajectory that increased the estimated risk of struggling with the bar exam.

Working part-time was the second most important factor, but it worked in your favor by pulling the prediction toward passing. Only 7% of accepted students planned to attend part-time, yet the model viewed this choice as reducing pressure and allowing more study time, which slightly improved your outlook.

Your first-year grades ranked third. This feature mildly supported passing, as your performance matched the typical level seen among students who were admitted.

Overall, the model saw the drop in your later academic performance as the dominant concern, outweighing the positive signals from your planned part-time schedule and solid start.

To strengthen future applications, focus on raising your LSAT score and undergraduate GPA, both of which sit below the averages of accepted students, and consider ways to demonstrate an upward trend in academic performance.
